e.etymology: A modern American name that follows Tamara and Amara with a K. Kamara is also a common West African surname in Sierra Leone, Guinea and Liberia.
An elaboration of Laura with an added A, close to Alora and Elora. Laura comes from Latin laurus, the laurel tree whose leaves crowned victors.
The Hebrew form of Zipporah, from tsippor, 'bird'. In Exodus she is the wife of Moses and a daughter of the Midianite priest Jethro.
A spelling of Waylon, itself a variant of Wayland, from Old English Weland, the master smith of Germanic legend. Country star Waylon Jennings made the name familiar.

assoc.t: Waylon Jennings, outlaw country singer (same sound)

e.etymology: A respelling of Jackson, an English surname meaning 'son of Jack'. Jack is a medieval pet form of John, from Hebrew Yochanan, 'God is gracious'.
A respelling of Shiloh, the Biblical town where the Ark of the Covenant rested before Jerusalem. The Hebrew is usually read as 'tranquil'; the name is also tied to the 1862 Civil War battle.

assoc.t: Battle of Shiloh, 1862 Civil War battle in Tennessee
Shiloh, the beagle of the children's novel and film

e.etymology: From Arabic husna, 'most beautiful' or 'best', the feminine superlative of hasan. The Quran uses it in al-asma al-husna, the most beautiful names of God.
From the surname Riggin, also seen as Riggins. Its use as a first name is recent and runs alongside Riggs and Riggins.
A Romanian name, most likely from soare, 'sun'. Soren, the Danish form of Latin Severinus, is a separate name with a similar sound.

assoc.t: Sorin Markov, vampire in Magic: The Gathering

e.etymology: An Indian name ending in raj, Sanskrit for 'king' or 'rule'. Indian name lists explain the first part as 'sun' and gloss the whole as a king who shines like the sun.
From the US state, named for the Sierra Nevada, Spanish for 'snow-covered mountains'. It was given to girls in the late 1800s, soon after statehood in 1864.

assoc.t: Nevada, US state, home of Las Vegas

e.etymology: The Hebrew form of Shiphrah, from a root meaning 'to be beautiful or pleasing'. In Exodus she is one of the two Hebrew midwives who defy Pharaoh's order to kill newborn boys.
From the Irish surname O hAonghusa, 'descendant of Aonghus (Angus)'. Irish emigre Richard Hennessy founded the cognac house that carries the name in 1765.
e.note: Best known as a cognac brand, so many people will hear a liquor reference.

e.etymology: A spelling of Kellen or Kellan, modern names drawn from Irish and Scottish surnames; the exact source is unsettled.
A respelling of Kinsley, an English surname from a Yorkshire place name, Old English for 'clearing of a man named Cyne', often rendered 'king's meadow'.
A modern American name in the pattern of Jayson, Kayson and Grayson. It also serves as a spelling of Tyson.
From an English surname for a reeve, the medieval steward or local official (Old English gerefa), with a later added -s.
From the English and Scottish surname for someone who lived by or worked at a mill.
namesakes: Mills Lane (boxing referee and TV judge)

e.etymology: A combination of Ella and Rose written as one word. Ella began as a Norman short form of Germanic names in ali, 'other', and is also a pet form of Ellen and Eleanor; Rose is the flower.
In American use a spelling of Mayla or Myla, modern names in the Mila and Kayla family. Maila is also a Finnish and Estonian name that began as a nursery form of Maria.
A modern South Asian name. In Muslim families it is a form of Arabic Rayyan, the gate of Paradise reserved for those who fast; it is also used as an Indian spelling of Ryan.
From Arabic ayat, the plural of aya, 'sign' or 'miracle', the word for the verses of the Quran. As a girls' name it is most common in Pakistan and India.
A pet form of Leonard, Germanic for 'brave as a lion', and for girls of Lenora, Leonie or Lennon. It is now given mainly to girls.
namesakes: Lennie Small (gentle giant of Steinbeck's Of Mice and Men)

assoc.t: Lennie Small in Steinbeck's Of Mice and Men

e.etymology: A pet form of Isaac, from Hebrew Yitzchak, 'he will laugh'. It was also the lifelong nickname of President Dwight D. Eisenhower, taken from his surname.
namesakes: Dwight Eisenhower (34th US president, nicknamed Ike)

assoc.t: Ike, nickname of President Dwight D. Eisenhower
Hurricane Ike, which struck the Texas coast in 2008
Mike and Ike, fruit-flavored chewy candy

e.etymology: An African American coinage that sets the prefix Ke- on Shawn, the anglicized Irish form of John. Keyshawn Johnson's NFL career in the late 1990s lifted the name.

e.meaning: Juan (God is gracious) joined with Carlos (free man)
e.etymology: The Spanish double name Juan Carlos written as one word. Juan is John, Hebrew for 'God is gracious', and Carlos is Charles, Germanic for 'free man'. Juan Carlos I was king of Spain from 1975 to 2014.
namesakes: Juan Carlos I (king of Spain, 1975 to 2014)

e.etymology: An African American coinage that adds the prefix De- to Marion, in the family of Demario, Demarcus and Jamarion.
A respelling of Amari, a name that came into wide American use in the 1990s. Its source is uncertain.
A feminine form of Emmanuel, from Hebrew Immanuel, 'God is with us', the name given in Isaiah's prophecy and applied to Jesus in Matthew's Gospel.
A modern name of unsettled origin, close in sound to Kalia, Kaliyah and Kehlani.

e.meaning: small, humble (from Paul), or of Apollo
e.etymology: The Russian form of French Pauline, from Latin Paulus, 'small'. It is also an old short form of Apollinariya, a name derived from the god Apollo.
From the English word, Old English snaw. Snow is also an old surname, first a nickname for someone with white hair or a pale complexion.

assoc.t: Jon Snow of Game of Thrones
President Snow of The Hunger Games
